paras: The threatened lynching of Louis Schlicht took place at Wausau, Wisconsin, on the night of January 1, 1888, when several hundred men surrounded the jail where Schlicht, a hotel keeper, was held for shooting Louis Butler. The crowd dispersed after Sheriff Healey warned that an armed posse would fire on any attempt, and Schlicht was later charged with first-degree murder. A wire report of the threatened lynching ran in papers from Minnesota to Texas.

Schlicht owned the Hotel Northern in Wausau and Butler owned the City Hotel. On New Year's Day Butler and five companions had been going from saloon to saloon, and Schlicht refused to serve the party drinks. According to witnesses at the later inquest, Schlicht shut the door on the group when they ordered drinks brought out to their sleigh, and they returned to his barroom at the urging of Charley Williams, who boarded at the hotel.

In the barroom, at about 6 p.m., insults passed between Butler and Schlicht, and the two men grappled. The witnesses testified that Butler had Schlicht's head under his arm when a pistol went off, and Butler "fell a corpse." Judge Marchetti, who was in an adjoining room, said Schlicht had thrown up his hands as if to warn Butler off and had retreated before shooting.

Schlicht went to the jail, surrendered himself, and handed his weapon to the sheriff. Several hundred men then surrounded the jail, "determined to lynch him," in the words of the wire report. Sheriff Healey declared that he had a posse armed with Winchesters and that any hostile attempt would be met with a volley, after which the crowd dispersed.

Coroner Quandt held an inquest in a crowded court house on January 3, and the jury recommended that Schlicht be held for trial. The Milwaukee Sentinel's report of the inquest said Schlicht called himself "a ruined man" and that public opinion on the shooting was divided; Butler was to be buried under the auspices of the Turnverein.

On January 13 Schlicht was bound over to the circuit court on a charge of first-degree murder; he claimed the shooting was accidental, though the St. Paul Daily Globe's correspondent wrote that "the evidence is against the plea." His bond was fixed at $4,000 on January 16, and he was expected to be released the next day. At his arraignment on March 27 he pleaded not guilty and was granted a continuance to the next term; no report of the trial's outcome was found.

The first reports came from a single wire dispatch dated January 1, which the Indianapolis Journal headed "Murder and Threatened Lynching" and the St. Paul Daily Globe "Wanted to Lynch Him." The dispatch was reprinted over the following days in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, the Indiana State Sentinel, the Indian Chieftain and the New Ulm Weekly Review, with the names spelled Schlitz, Schilitz, Schlicht or Schilcht and, in Fort Worth, a "Warsaw" dateline and a "Larry Butler." The dispatch reported the crowd's purpose and the sheriff's warning without comment.

Weekly news summaries cut the story to a line or two. The Great Falls Tribune and the Worthington Advance kept the lynching threat, the latter calling Schlicht "the Wausau, Wis., murderer" who was "saved from lynching only by a strong guard," while the Kanabec County Times, the Stark County Democrat and the River Falls Journal mentioned only the shooting. The Wisconsin coverage of the inquest, reprinted in the Wood County Reporter from the Sentinel, gave the witnesses' detailed account of the struggle but did not mention the crowd at the jail. Later Wausau specials in the St. Paul Daily Globe followed the case through the courts, one calling Schlicht "the murderer of Butler" before his trial.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Louis Schlicht
bases: Several hundred men surrounded the Wausau jail 'determined to lynch' Schlicht, who was held for killing Louis Butler, and dispersed when the sheriff threatened them with an armed posse (A1, A2, A9).

No one was killed by the crowd: several hundred men gathered at the jail intending to lynch Schlicht for the killing of Butler, but dispersed after the sheriff's warning (A1, A2); it was a threatened lynching only.

The jail crowd appears in one wire report carried by many papers (A1, A2) and in separately worded briefs (A9, A11); the shooting itself is confirmed by the local inquest report and later court reports (A5, A13, A16), though no local account of the crowd was found.
